lines: That correctness guarantee from last time leans on one thing surviving a restart: the place that actually holds a running total between triggers.
Here's what that place is, and when the obvious choice for it stops being enough.
By default, that place is a plain object, sitting in the same memory the rest of the program uses.
One object per key being tracked. A handful of keys, nothing to notice. Millions of keys, millions of those objects, all living in the one spot the garbage collector has to walk.
Here's a question worth sitting with before the answer comes.
Grow that key count toward a million, still on the default place. Does the time spent collecting garbage stay flat, or does it climb along with the key count?
steps.answer: It climbs. More live objects for the collector to walk, every single pass.

lines: Climbs, and measured directly.
The default place pays real, climbing collection time as the key count grows. Hand the identical workload to the other option, and that cost barely moves.
Here's why one option stays flat where the other doesn't.
It keeps those millions of entries somewhere else entirely -- not program memory, but space the collector was never built to look at in the first place.
Here's a different kind of question.
Every time progress gets saved, does the whole running state get written out again from scratch, or is there a cheaper way that writes less than everything?
steps.answer: There's a cheaper way. Only what changed gets written, not the whole thing again.

lines: There's a cheaper way, and it's measured, not assumed.
Turn that option on, and the amount written per save collapses -- same workload, same data, a fraction of the bytes.
Here's the part that doesn't go away.
The expensive full write still happens eventually, in the background. The cheaper option only puts it off -- it never skips it for good.
Here's a fact worth sitting with on the way out.
Every single example run in this entire chapter stayed nowhere near the point where any of this actually mattered.
Two ways of holding the same running state, and one real question between them.
Does a growing key count ever become the collector's own problem, or does it never reach that far at all?
